extracted.intended_audience: machine learning researchers, conference organizers, and peer reviewers concerned with reproducibility of ML experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what kinds of reproducibility are appropriate for different kinds of ML experimental claims, and concrete items that methods-focused reproducibility checklists typically require. Aimed at aligning reproducibility requirements to claim scope and ethical risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods reproducibility (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting the same results when implementing the same computational procedures on the same data, typically including access to the original code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the dominant conception in ML venues; checklists and programs emphasize making code and data accessible and stating metrics/parameters used. Methods reproducibility is a bare minimum for many experiments but may be insufficient for broader claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results reproducibility (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generating statistically similar results when re-implementing a method (i.e., obtaining comparable numerical outcomes under independent reimplementation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from methods reproducibility and inferential reproducibility; relevant when assessing whether independent implementations reproduce performance magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferential reproducibility (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing the same conclusion or finding from a different experimental setup (i.e., reproducing the inference/interpretation rather than only numeric outputs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims that are interpretive or causal, inferential reproducibility (akin to conceptual replication) is often required to substantiate the scientific claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability vs reproducibility (terminology note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different authors swap meanings: Peng intended 'replicability' as using original code and 'reproducibility' as independent re-implementation, while others reverse these terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about definitions used in any checklist or review to avoid confusion; expectation: clarify whether original code runs are enough or independent reimplementations are expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs conceptual replication (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct replication uses similar protocol/materials to the original; conceptual replication uses different protocols/materials aimed at testing the same underlying claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual replication is similar to inferential reproducibility and is important when the claim's scope extends beyond the original experimental context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference methods-reproducibility checklist items
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete items emphasized by ML conference checklists (e.g., NeurIPS, AAAI, EMNLP) for methods reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should provide datasets, code, hyper-parameters, number of training/evaluation runs, definitions of metrics used, and computing infrastructure. Reproducibility programs often focus on producing same results with same data and code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match reproducibility standard to claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproducibility standards should vary depending on what kind of claim the paper is making (from proof-of-concept to claims about scientific hypotheses or broad method superiority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods reproducibility is the minimum; broader claims require stronger forms (e.g., reproducibility across datasets, conceptual replications, inferential reproducibility). Reviewers and checklists should ask authors to state claim scope explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility requirements for Method Superiority claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is that a novel method is superior for a class of problems, reproducibility should show success across representative problems and rule out confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproduce under different computational power and hyperparameter optimization regimes (within the stated range of where the method is optimal) to avoid spurious superiority due to unequal tuning. Demonstrate performance across a representative sample of problems/datasets/tasks (not only a single benchmark like ImageNet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility requirements for Theoretical Virtues claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming that a particular theoretical property of a method explains its superior performance, reproductions must show that the property is causally responsible for the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform controlled variants/ablations that add or remove the alleged virtue and compare performance. Implement the virtue in multiple ways and show consistent improvements across conditions and comparisons to methods lacking the virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility requirements for Proof-of-Concept claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs of concept show that a method could be useful for a task; these are the weakest claims and methods reproducibility may suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rerunning the original code with the same dataset to obtain similar results can be adequate, but the limits of generalizability should be acknowledged; demonstrating broader generalization requires additional tests (different datasets, compute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility requirements for Scientific Hypotheses claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When ML experiments are used to support scientific (natural or social) hypotheses, methods reproducibility alone is insufficient; we need to ensure the model reflects relevant real-world features rather than dataset quirks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require inferential reproducibility or conceptual replications: use different datasets, different operationalizations of constructs, and validations of construct validity and construct repeatability. Rule out preprocessing or data-collection artifacts and demonstrate that findings are robust under changes that should be irrelevant to the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility requirements for Quantifying Predictability claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When ML is used to quantify how predictable a phenomenon is, the required reproducibility depends on the scope of the claim (specific dataset vs phenomenon generally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If scope is narrow (predictability from a specific dataset), methods reproducibility may suffice; if scope is broad (predictability in general), require reproducibility across diverse datasets and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical risk should raise reproducibility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Research that carries higher societal risk (e.g., reviving physiognomy, predicting sexual orientation) ought to meet more stringent reproducibility and evidentiary standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical considerations motivate requiring inference-focused replications, better construct validation, multiple datasets, and possibly higher evidentiary thresholds before accepting sensitive claims. The paper cites Wang & Kosinski (2018) as an example where methods reproducibility alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require authors to specify claim scope and consider pre-registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers often leave implicit the scope of their claims; reproducibility expectations depend on that scope, so authors should state it explicitly (potentially via pre-registration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-evaluate publication norms to require clarity about the intended scope of claims; consider pre-registration so reviewers and readers can judge whether the appropriate level of reproducibility has been provided.
